texts: A shirt has no skeleton: how our garment forge rigs a piece in 7 stages, then lifts the body out

A shirt has no skeleton, so our garment forge rigs each piece while a reference body is wearing it, then removes the body and keeps the weights the cloth picked up from the joints underneath. The write-up follows one real shirt through the seven stages and the gates a piece passes before it is published: three.ws/wardrobe

A region counts as covered when it carries 10% or more of the weight

the record of a job in storage is also its work queue
An instance owns a job only once it holds a concurrency slot and wins an atomic, generation-matched write on the record
Everything the pipeline needs is stored at submit, so any instance can drive a job it did not receive
A freed slot drains the backlog straight away, a sweep every 10 minutes claims any orphan, and a job read requeues one whose owner went quiet

A job is declared failed only after three attempts, so a replaced instance costs an attempt, not the piece
A submit takes one attempt, because it starts a GPU job and is not safely repeatable; a read takes three
the page saves the job id in the browser, so a visitor who closes the tab at minute three finds the job still running on return
